questions.q: What three ingredients does the summary say combine to create luck?
a: Talent, chance and hard work
Wealth, education and social class
Optimism, patience and good timing
Skill, luck and family connections
questions.why: The overview compares luck to three cherries lining up: talent, chance and hard work.

questions.q: What happened to John Grisham before his first legal thriller was published?
a: Twenty-eight publishers rejected it
He rewrote it for more than a decade
He published it himself at his own expense
An agent discovered it at a writing contest
questions.why: Lesson 1 says Grisham submitted the manuscript to 28 publishers before a small house accepted it.

questions.q: What did Dick Fosbury's story illustrate about luck?
a: Persistence with a new idea can outlast ridicule
Natural athletic talent matters more than technique
Coaches usually recognize innovation immediately
Success depends on competing in the right country
questions.why: Lesson 1 says Fosbury kept practicing his backward jump despite mockery and eventually won Olympic gold.

questions.q: What does the hockey advice to skate where the puck will be mean for luck?
a: Put yourself in places where opportunities gather
Wait for a clear opportunity before making a move
Practice your skills until you are the very best
Follow the career path that others recommend
questions.why: Lesson 2 says you must step outside your comfort zone and go where opportunities are likely to appear.

questions.q: Which connections does the summary say are often most valuable for creating luck?
a: Weak ties with people you see only occasionally
Close family members who know you well
Former employers and direct supervisors
Friends who share your profession and interests
questions.why: Lesson 3 says weak connections matter most because they link you to different circles of people.
